title: Terry Mikeska Foundation supplies hope for Nepal - gosanangelo.com
description: Terry Mikeska Foundation supplies hope for Nepal  gosanangelo.com
publisher.title: gosanangelo.com
full_article:
What happens when your home country suffers a catastrophe of biblical proportions and you are thousands of miles away?

On the morning of Aug. 26, Bijaya Deuja, a nurse born and raised in Nepal who has worked in San Angelo, learned of the 5.2 earthquake and the horror of the massive Himalayan glacier collapse that triggered an avalanche and flash flood.

“I first tried to call my parents who still live there but was unable to get through," Deuja said. "I had better luck on social media where I was able to contact family. I was told that my parents and family were safe and physically intact but horribly traumatized by the disaster. As a nurse, I felt helpless knowing that I could not help.”

A life of service

In fact, Deuja is no stranger to trauma.

“My life in Nepal was always about service. I got my degree in nursing and counseling and then spent 10 years as a police officer in the Army assigned to the Peace Keeping Bureau of the United Nations," she said.

"There I worked as a counselor and nurse in Haiti during the earthquake of 2018. It has been stressful to think of the same trauma affecting people in Nepal," Deuja said.

In 2022, Deuja’s life of service also brought her to San Angelo. With a master’s degree of science in nursing, a master’s degree in political science and a master’s degree in sociology, she spent four years in surgical oncology at Shannon Medical Center in San Angelo.

“I came to the United States as the land of opportunity, and I know that so many in Nepal will never get that chance," Deuja said.

"But the people of Nepal are a hopeful people, and I have felt hopeful knowing what my friend, San Angeloan Terry Mikeska, is doing, she said. "He has been a blessing for the people of Nepal. I have never met someone so generous."

Terry Mikeska Foundation seeks to help

According to Mikeska, CEO of the Terry Mikeska Foundation, it was the disaster of the earthquake of 2015 in Nepal that inspired him to start his foundation. “I looked at the pictures of the devastation and felt like I had to do something.”

Since that first visit to Nepal 11 years ago, the foundation, through its connection with Christian groups in Nepal, has built two schools and six Christian churches, delivered more than 5,000 Bibles, hundreds of rice pots and thousands of bags of rice, including backpacks, clothing and shoes for more than 5,000 children.

The foundation has built wells and installed filtration systems, upgraded and installed restrooms, including providing feminine hygiene products to women that were often banned based on ancient Hindu traditions.

Within hours after hearing about the disaster, Mikeska had made contact with foundation volunteers on the ground.

“Pastor Amosh Khadka, one of the more than 100 Christian leaders I have recruited over the years, is on the ground now sending me photos and giving me firsthand information as to what people need the most. Here is his report from Sept. 2,” said Mikeska.

“In the flood-affected area of Bidur Municipality, Ward No. 9, Nuwakot district, impacted by the Bhote Koshi River, I have distributed essential food supplies including rice, lentils, oil, and salt, along with clothing. Thank you so much for your prayers and support that is bringing renewed hope and a fresh lease on life to these flood survivors,” Khadka said.

Mikeska said, “There is almost nothing that can be salvaged from before the flood. Everything must be purchased and brought in from neighboring areas.”

Because it is not feasible to ship goods into the area, the Terry Mikeska Foundation is now fundraising dollars for Nepal.

“Our Foundation is experienced with providing aid to Nepal and the people of San Angelo have always been generous and eager to help," Mikeska said. "We can make a difference right away.”

The website for giving is www.terrymikeskafoundation.org. Mikeska can be reached at tjmikeska@icloud.com for more information. The Foundation will continue to update its website on the status of the work and how donations have been used.

title: More than 5,700 people missing in Nepal a month after floods — Dawn - ua.news
description: More than 5,700 people missing in Nepal a month after floods — Dawn  ua.news
publisher.title: ua.news
full_article:
One month after the devastating flood in Nepal, caused by the collapse of ice and rock on Mount Langtang Lirung, rescuers have recovered 1,451 bodies, while more than 5,700 people are considered missing. Dawn reports, citing Nepal’s disaster response authorities.

The collapse occurred on August 26 on the northern slope of Mount Langtang Lirung near the China-Nepal border. According to geologist Sudan Bikash Maharjan of the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, the mass of ice and rock came down from an altitude of about 5,200 meters. The debris traveled approximately 20 kilometers and descended 1,700 meters into the Rasuwagadhi area in just seven minutes.

Search and identification of the dead

Those missing include hundreds of workers on hydropower projects, as well as foreigners, including tourists and pilgrims. The identification of victims is complicated by the need for DNA testing. Due to overloaded morgues, many bodies were buried in mass graves after DNA data had been recorded. So far, the identities of about 100 victims have been established.

On the Chinese side of the border, state media reported 43 deaths and 519 people missing. Hundreds of rescuers, some of whom were delivered by helicopter, continue searching through mud and debris. In Nepal, three workers — two Nepalese and a Chinese citizen — were rescued from tunnels under construction. One of them, 30-year-old Sanjay Sah, told AFP that he survived 10 days in darkness by drinking muddy water.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Aid and damage

The disaster affected more than 80,000 people, with thousands living in temporary shelters. The UN has appealed for nearly $50 million in emergency aid. Some communities near the epicenter remain cut off, so the UN and Nepalese authorities are delivering supplies there by helicopters and cargo drones.

Nepal estimates the cost of reconstruction at $4.78 billion, of which $57 million is needed over the next six months for short-term recovery. The flood reduced the country’s total generating capacity by 10%, mainly because of damage to hydropower facilities. The energy sector accounts for half of all infrastructure damage.

Scientists from World Weather Attribution called the disaster a “compound crisis” linked to prolonged warming, glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and geological instability. Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, said climate change was one of the factors in the tragedy.

title: China hands over MAZU weather forecasting model to Nepal. Also deployed in Pakistan - ThePrint
description: China hands over MAZU weather forecasting model to Nepal. Also deployed in Pakistan  ThePrint
publisher.title: ThePrint
full_article:
The 26 August floods originated from a glacial rock collapse in the Lhende Khola R iver on the Tibet-Nepal border, and travelled down to the Bhote K oshi R iver, which entered Nepal in the northern Rasuwa district. The first few villages at the Rasuwa-Tibet border had no warning of the deluge, and many people, houses, and bridges were swept away within seconds.

During the post-flood analysis period, Nepali authorities, including the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), pointed out that there was little to no glacial, meteorological, or hydrological information being exchanged between China and Nepal, despite Nepal being downstream of many rivers that originate in China.

“In the aftermath (of the floods), CMA (China Meteorological Administration) provided continuous meteorological support to Nepal, conducting joint video consultations and supplying forecasting and warning products,” said the press release by the CMA .

MAZU was built on a trial basis after the flood

Three days after the floods, when the glacial lake formed by the ice rock collapse showed signs of bursting, China sent warnings to Nepal inform ing the nation of a possible second flood. The two countries also agreed on information-sharing in the event of natural disasters ; however, no formal bilateral mechanism has been established yet .

The MAZU platform was built on a trial basis in the week following the flood, and was provided to Nepali officials through cloud servers. The CMA used it to produce daily monitoring bulletins and reports for Nepal, as the platform integrated satellite observations with Chinese forecasting models such as Fengqing and Fengshun, while also being tailored for Nepal’s geography.

Now, China plans to deploy the MAZU-Fengyun satellite AI box and other equipment to Nepal, and also conduct training sessions for Nepali meteorologists and other engineers to use the system efficiently. Since Nepal does not have its own meteorological satellite system currently , this tool will allow the country to monitor and evaluate its natural disaster risk, as well as other weather-based phenomenon.

MAZU has also been customised for Pakistan and will soon be deployed in other Central Asian countries, as announced in the Forum.

title: Some Nepal Acts being amended for effective disaster response management - Khabarhub
description: Some Nepal Acts being amended for effective disaster response management  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The government is proposing amendment to some Nepal Acts to make disaster response further effective.

In this connection, the Ministry of Home Affairs has prepared a ‘Bill to Amend Some Nepal Acts Related to Disasters.’

The bill has been prepared to make arrangement for search, mortuary storage, and handover of the bodies of people losing lives in disasters; minimum relief to families of missing persons, and judicial declaration of death in case the missing person is not found.

The ministry has currently published a notice under the Legislative Act, 2081, seeking public opinion regarding the bill.

People are requested to send their suggestions or inputs via email to [email protected] within seven days of the notice publication.

According to the ministry, the bill amends the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, 2074, by adding Clause 33 (a) after Clause 33. The Clause specifies arrangements for the search, storage, and handover of the bodies of people who die due to serious natural disasters.

The proposed amendment will make arrangements for the minimum relief to be provided to the families of those missing due to disasters.

The government has added Section 4 after Section 3 of the restrictive phrase in Clause 40(1)(1) of the Civil Code, 2074.

If a person goes missing in such a disaster and is not found, the Government of Nepal is not required to issue a judicial declaration of death according to the prevailing law, the bill states.

The amendment is also proposed in the National Identity Card and Registration Act, 2076. If there is no guardian assigned under Clause (B), the person’s guardian according to prevailing law, or their guardian-in-law, or if such a person does not exist, the head of the local level or the chairperson of the relevant ward should make the declaration.

In case of a foreign citizen who dies or goes missing in natural disaster, the embassy or consulate of the relevant country appointed in Nepal or overseeing Nepal should make the declaration.

Additionally, special arrangements are provided for the registration of events of persons missing due to disasters.

If a person missing in disaster is not found during search and rescue once the declared disaster period ends or search and rescue operations conclude, the person can report the death to the registrar’s office of the local level where the person has a permanent address or temporary residence, or where the incident occurred, along with the required documents. title: At the UN, Shah to bring Nepal’s climate crisis into focus - The Kathmandu Post
description: At the UN, Shah to bring Nepal’s climate crisis into focus  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, the world’s youngest national leader and head of government, is set to address one of the world’s oldest international institutions in New York.

According to a June 2026 analysis by the Pew Research Center covering leaders of 186 UN member states, Shah is currently the world’s youngest national leader and head of government. He will use the United Nations General Assembly, one of the world’s biggest annual diplomatic gatherings, to highlight the climate crisis and its consequences for vulnerable countries.

The address is part of Shah’s first foreign visit since he became prime minister on March 27.

The recent flash floods in the Bhotekoshi river and their devastating impact downstream have prompted the prime minister to use the UN’s highest-level international platform to draw global attention to the disaster’s toll on lives and livelihoods, as well as infrastructure, hydropower and other socioeconomic sectors.

The death toll from the catastrophic flash floods along the Bhotekoshi river reached 1,452 as of September 23, while search teams continue to look for 4,718 people who remain missing, including several hundred foreign nationals.

Shah is scheduled to address the General Debate of the 81st UN General Assembly on Thursday afternoon in New York, or after midnight in Nepal early Friday. According to the UN’s published schedule, his session begins at 3pm New York time.

In his address, Shah is expected to highlight the devastating consequences of the Bhotekoshi disaster and the growing vulnerability of Himalayan communities to climate-induced disasters.

Nepal is expected to argue that countries that have contributed relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions should not be left to bear the financial and human costs of a climate crisis they did little to create. Shah is expected to call for greater international support for disaster preparedness, climate resilience, reconstruction and rehabilitation.

He is also expected to press for greater access to climate finance, technology and capacity-building support, as well as an effective loss-and-damage mechanism to assist vulnerable countries without adding to their debt burden.

The Bhotekoshi disaster, which devastated communities in Rasuwa and downstream areas, has added urgency to Nepal’s climate diplomacy at this year’s General Assembly. Nepal has sought international assistance for recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction following the disaster.

Shah is also expected to underline the particular vulnerability of mountain countries, where rising temperatures, melting glaciers, changing precipitation patterns and other climate-related risks threaten lives, livelihoods and infrastructure.

The prime minister arrived in New York on Wednesday, leading the Nepali delegation to the General Assembly. He is scheduled to meet UN Secretary-General António Guterres during his stay.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has been participating in high-level meetings, side events and bilateral engagements in New York since September 20.

The theme of this year’s General Assembly is “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All.” The General Debate is being held from September 22 to 26 and on September 28.

Shah’s appearance at the UN comes nearly six months after he assumed office and marks his first foreign visit as prime minister. His delegation includes Foreign Minister Khanal, Chief Adviser Kumar Byanjankar, Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai and other senior government officials.

KATHMANDU — Nepal’s rapper-turned-prime minister swept to power six months ago on a wave of youth-led anti-corruption protests, buoyed by optimism for change.

Now Balendra Shah faces his biggest test as his country’s leader after a catastrophic flood on the China-Nepal border killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing.

The disaster has pushed climate diplomacy to the centre of the 36-year-old’s premiership, overshadowing the anti-corruption agenda that powered his rise to office.

Shah is due to address the United Nations General Assembly this week, using his first foreign trip as prime minister to press Nepal’s case for greater international support to recover from a disaster scientists have linked to climate change.

Shah has called the “unimaginable and heartbreaking” flood “not an ordinary” event, warning that it demonstrates the growing dangers facing communities across the Himalayas.

When floodwaters surged through his area on August 26, nine-year-old Ram Thakur was climbing uphill with his mother and dozens of other people trying to escape. Looking back, he saw muddy water rising behind them, and the group began to run. His mother, who had been holding his hand, pushed him to climb faster and shouted at him in Nepali to keep going and not look back.

He did as she said and kept climbing. When he finally turned around, the water was still churning nearby, but his mother was gone.

Almost four weeks later, Thakur is still hoping his mother and father will come for him. He now lives with 26 other children in a government primary school in Nuwakot district that has been converted into a temporary shelter.

align-items: center;margin-top:16px;}

That leaves Thakur and the others in limbo. On paper, they are not orphans. In reality, they have been without their parents since the floods, which killed more than 1,400 people and left at least 5,000 missing.

Children displaced by the deadly flash floods and mudslide, stand in a queue to receive free clothes at a school turned into a temporary shelter, in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, September 5, 2026. REUTERS/Adnan Abidi

Waiting for His Parents

August 26 started as a normal school day for Thakur. He was walking to school with his mother around 8 a.m. when disaster struck. His father, a guide and driver who started work at 10 a.m., was still at home.

googletag.cmd.push(function() { googletag.display('300x250_middle_2'); });

googletag.cmd.push(function() { googletag.display('300x250_m2'); });

Then people began yelling at them to run because a flood was coming. Thakur and his mother walked, climbed and ran until they were separated. He spent a day stranded on a hill with 13 others before an army helicopter rescued them. He said he was terrified and hungry and feared he would die, adding that his school bag with his biscuits and lunchbox had been swept away.

Eating a lunch of lentils, rice and greens with the other children at the shelter, Thakur said he could not understand why his parents had not come to find him yet. He said they both knew how to swim, so they should have arrived by now.

A counselor at the shelter said Thakur still rushes outside every time he hears a helicopter, hoping his parents have been rescued.

A post-flood assessment carried out this month by Nepal’s National Child Rights Council and Save the Children found more than 1,000 children living in temporary shelters. Of these, more than 100 had no relatives with them, and 439 were without their parents but had other family members present, said Ayush Joshi, program director for Save the Children in Nepal.

googletag.cmd.push(function() { googletag.display('300x250_middle_3'); });

Overall, the floods displaced more than 32,000 children, according to Leon Muwoni, head of child protection at UNICEF Nepal. Officials and aid groups are working to trace their families, and so far 18 children have been reunited with their parents.

Corn sprouts from mud-covered storage inside the home of Chiranjivi Pudasaini, 54, alongside a toy doll belonging to his granddaughter, a week after flash floods and mudslides struck Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, September 9, 2026. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu

Silent From Shock

Thakur’s shelter has eight rooms. Local nonprofits have set up six of them with waterproof mats, bedding and stuffed toys, and workers are building bunk beds. One room stores food supplies and another serves as a kitchen. Most of the staff are Nepal police officers, and the rest work for nonprofits, along with one counselor. All of them are women.

About 100 kilometers (60 miles) away, at a children’s shelter in Dhading, four-year-old Shibani Tama has stopped speaking. Both of her parents have been confirmed dead.

Caregivers say she remembers little about her neighborhood or her relatives, and no family members have come for her. The only thing she has told rescuers and counselors is that she was at school when teachers hurried her and other students uphill.

Yamuna Bhattarai, a caregiver at the shelter, said Shibani does not talk to anyone, will not let anyone comb her hair and only allows her clothes to be changed every two or three days after a lot of coaxing. She said it is deeply upsetting to see Shibani and other children in such severe shock, and that all of them urgently need psychological support.

Children displaced by the flash floods and mudslide, look at a mobile phone as they take shelter inside a hospital, at Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 30, 2026. REUTERS/Adnan Abidi

Children Caring for Children

Many children who lost both parents never learned to wash their hair, change their clothes or feed themselves. Others are now looking after younger siblings despite being young themselves.

Ten-year-old Sanju Lama was heading to her grandmother’s home in Rasuwa, the district hardest hit by the floods, with her two-year-old brother when strangers grabbed them and pulled them to safety. Floodwaters swallowed her home, and her parents, who were expected to be home at the time, are missing.

Bhattarai said loud noises startle Sanju, even someone calling her name. She holds her little brother’s hand almost constantly and often wakes up frightened at night. She spends much of the day reading English poems to him. According to Bhattarai, the two now have only each other.

UNICEF says 18 schools in the affected districts were destroyed and another 20 were damaged, leaving children without safe places to learn, play and heal. Dozens of schools sit near riverbanks and remain at risk, and an estimated 10,000 school-age children face an uncertain future in education.

Support Falling Short

Aid workers, counselors and childcare staff at school shelters in Dhading say their efforts to help the children feel safe often are not enough. Toys, books and games have been handed out, but few children use them. Many remain withdrawn, distracted or too overwhelmed to play.

Joshi said Save the Children has provided toys and school supplies to children in the shelters. In some cases, volunteers have seen children whose parents are missing using dollhouses to create families with parents. He said the children likely do not grasp what has happened or why, and have no sense of what tomorrow or the future will bring.

Many children are living in crowded shelters with little privacy. At the same time, officials and aid groups say they must be cautious about releasing children to people claiming to be relatives. Muwoni said some children whose relatives have been found are being kept in shelters when those relatives cannot provide enough documentation or proof of guardianship, to protect them from trafficking and child labor.

In Nepal, the law has eliminated gender discrimination when it comes to property rights, but cultural norms still interfere with land ownership.

Many of the country’s agricultural workers are women, yet they do not own the land they work.

Research shows that globally, women’s access to secure land tenure is linked to higher agricultural productivity, lower food insecurity, reduced poverty and slower environmental degradation.

POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm.

Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s a common scenario in Nepal, where gendered divisions of agricultural labor are widespread.

For Bishwokaarma, that meant she and her mother grew maize, potatoes, garlic and other vegetables. She participated in the entire agricultural cycle, from preparing fields and planting crops to harvesting them. She enjoyed plowing the most, but it was physically demanding because the family lacked modern machinery.

“We didn’t have tractors,” she said. “So, everything, start to ending, we had to do with our own hands. It was really hard.”

It’s what many women and girls experience. And yet, their prospects for owning the land they tend are slim: Despite gender equality under the law, in Nepal, property rights rest mostly with men.

Still, it’s women — accounting for nearly 70% of the country’s farming population — whom Bishwokaarma credits most with caring for the land. Throughout her childhood, she saw how dedicated women were to conserving their environment. She explained that many women learn from childhood how to keep the soil healthy and reduce pests naturally through mixed cropping, crop rotation and intercropping.

Farmers harvest paddy at Bhaktapur, Nepal. Agriculture is the main source of food, income and employment for the majority of people in Nepal, yet the majority of land ownership is concentrated among men. Image by AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha.

But these aren’t the only techniques women in Nepal use to take care of the land they use. Bishwokaarma said women use farmyard manure made from cow or buffalo dung, compost from kitchen waste and plant residues instead of chemical fertilizer. They even use natural pesticides made from neem leaves, garlic, chiles, ash, cow urine or local herbs to reduce insect damage. Around the fields, they plant flowers and local plants that attract bees, butterflies and other pollinators to help increase crop production as well.

To Bishwokaarma, women play a vital role in protecting land through agricultural practices.

“The men don’t know the exact process of farming,” she said. “Women dedicate their life to the land, and I have seen that my mother, aunts, my friends, were all experts in every agriculture process—yet all of the property, our house, our land, everything is in my father’s name.”

The imbalance Bishwokaarma describes extends well beyond her family.

The National Agricultural Census of 2021-22 found that just 20.8% of adult women involved in farming in Nepal have secure ownership rights to agricultural land, compared with 42.9% of men. Traditional gender-based divisions in agricultural work are also still common, although widespread male out-migration has forced a shift in these roles, often increasing the physical burden on women.

The inequalities in land tenure are not unique to Nepal, and they reflect a broader pattern that extends beyond the country’s borders.

Binita Bishwokaarma attends a Model United Nations competition. Image courtesy of Binita Bishwokaarma.

Global gender imbalance

Across the Global South, women play a central role in agriculture while continuing to face unequal access to land and property rights. Globally, women account for less than 20% of landholders, and only 37% of countries guarantee equal land rights for women and men, according to U.N. figures.

Yet studies show that women’s access to secure land tenure is linked to higher agricultural productivity, lower food insecurity, reduced poverty and slower environmental degradation. A 2024 global evidence review by the nonprofit Landesa revealed growing evidence that secure land rights also help women adapt to climate change while supporting sustainable forest management and conservation.

George Washington University has reported similar findings. An international law and policy brief covering Ecuador, Mexico, Nepal and Peru stated that secure land ownership is associated with lower deforestation and more successful reforestation. In Uganda and Ethiopia, researchers found landholders with secure tenure were more likely to invest in soil conservation and climate resilience.

Plus, the benefits of land ownership go beyond individual women. “When women have access and rights to land, the economic benefits extend to their households and their communities,” the World Resources Institute reported, pointing to research showing women contribute more of their income to the household than men do, thereby improving education, health and food security for children.

Despite all this, land ownership remains dominated by men, even nonagricultural land. When it comes to Nepal, men are roughly twice as likely to own property, with only about 11% of women owning land overall.

“Even now, the modern law and Constitution give full rights to women, but it’s not implemented properly,” said Tanuja Pariyar, project coordinator in Pokhara, Kaski district, for the Feminist Dalit Organization (FEDO), an NGO dedicated to fighting caste- and gender-based discrimination.

A Nepal woiman separates chaff from wheat on the outskirts of Kathmandu, Nepal. Despite their work in agriculture, many women in Nepal do not have land rights. Image by AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha.

Nepal has introduced a series of legal reforms over the past two decades to reduce gender disparities in land ownership. In 2002, the 11th amendment to the civil code granted daughters a share of ancestral property by birth, but women still lost those rights upon marriage. That was changed in 2017, when legal gender-based discrimination in property inheritance was eliminated.

However, these legal reforms haven’t changed social norms that continue to shape who controls land and who benefits from it. By 2011, about 19% of households reported women owning land or property, but many women remained excluded from key decisions.

“For property decisions from taking a loan to selling something, most of the time the decisions are taken by the man,” Pariyar said.

Pariyar’s comment is bolstered by research that shows gender imbalances in decision-making powers within farming regions can harm not only women — but the community as a whole. “When women lack the tools, information and decision-making authority needed to implement adaptive strategies, the resilience of entire farming systems is compromised,” according to a 2025 study in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems .

“Nepal is a patriarchal system because it’s a historical system,” Pariyar said. “This is a male-dominated society, and they don’t want to give power to women because they don’t trust it. That is the first issue.”

A Nepali farmer plants paddy saplings on the outskirts of Kathmandu. Many women in Nepal work in agriculture, but men hold the majority of land rights. Image by AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha.

Patriarchal expectations

For women like Bishwokaarma, who is now a law student, those norms were learned early.

Although she worked closely with the land, she and many other women were taught from a young age that neither the family home nor the land belonged to them. Instead, all of the property belonged to the men in the family. Since she was raised in a patriarchal household where most major decisions were made by her father, she grew up surrounded by traditional beliefs and social norms that shaped expectations about ownership. Even though women are not legally barred from owning land today, these expectations often discouraged them from pursuing ownership.

As she grew older, Bishwokaarma began to see how those expectations affected her own mother. She said her mother often expressed frustration that despite years of laboring for the family, she remained dependent on her husband because she lacked property and financial security of her own that restricted her from making important financial decisions.

“It’s human nature because when you do lots of hard work and you never get appreciated for that work, obviously you get frustrated,” Bishwokaarma said. “That’s why she told me to get an education and become independent on my own.”

For advocates working on women’s rights in Nepal, that kind of independence begins with schooling.

Rabina G. Rasaily, FEDO executive director, says educating women is important when it comes to land ownership and its benefits. In her view, ownership is about more than legal rights. It can influence access to resources, decision-making power and economic security. Rasaily said that when women gain access to land, the benefits can positively affect future generations through improvements in health, an increase in educational opportunities and an increase in investments in homes and businesses.

These benefits also extend into conservation in Nepal. WRI research shows that in Banpale Community Forest, where women are guaranteed rights to the communal land, women have been inspired to actively participate in sustainable forestry and engage in climate adaptation training. These trainings include forest fire management, water conservation, landslide and soil erosion preventions and human-wildlife conflict avoidance strategies.

(Left) Tanuja Pariyar, project coordinator of FEDO Kaski district, poses for a portrait in Pokhara, Nepal. Pariyar helps marginalized women’s groups that are facing difficulties with property rights. (Right) Rabina G. Rasaily, FEDO executive director, has more than 15 years of experience in social justice movements across Nepal. Images courtesy of Peter Murray.

Understanding their rights

Realizing those benefits often depends on women understanding the rights available to them — yet many women do not, Rasaily said.

“There were some times when we’d have conversations and they would say, ‘Oh really? We can even own land, or property or a building?’” Rasaily said. “It’s beyond their thinking sometimes.”

However, the lack of individual ownership is not always viewed as a problem by women living within the system. For some, security comes through the family rather than personal ownership, which was the case for 28-year-old Mamta Kaushal.

Kaushal grew up with her two sisters and brother in the rural village of Tadapani in Nepal’s Annapurna region. She married at 18 and moved 50 kilometers (30 miles) to Pokhara city, to live on her husband’s property. The house and land where she now lives are ancestral property that have been passed down through generations. Although the property is not registered in her name, Kaushal said she doesn’t see it as a bad thing — she views it as a shared resource.

“It doesn’t matter, the name or register in which family member it is in,” she said. “Because we are in the same family.”

Kaushal works the family’s land. She grows plants like maize, wheat and potatoes throughout the seasons when the soil isn’t resting from the last crop and raises buffaloes on parts of their land. Kaushal sees her work as her duty to contribute to the family’s financial stability, provide food security to her family and keep the land productive through cultivation in order to preserve it for future generations.

For women who do want to acquire their own property, Kaushal expressed how access to property is less of a concern than it once was. She said she has not personally seen many women struggle to acquire property on their own because women can now earn income through wage labor or selling produce, textiles and clothing.

Mamta Kaushal and other women in Pokhara, Nepal, walk to the fields behind their homes to check on their crops of maize. Many women share and rent land for agricultural production to support their families and sell produce for profit. Image courtesy of Peter Murray.

Kaushal also said women have greater opportunities to purchase land independently through a reduction in property registration fees the Nepal government offers for land registered in a woman’s name. Through this discount, women get 25-50% off fees associated with land purchases or transfers, rather than reducing annual property taxes. The rebate aims to empower women by incentivizing them to hold land ownership.

For Bishwokaarma, however, the issue is not whether women can own land, but whether they are encouraged and supported in doing so.

“Personally, I hope that more women in Nepal will not only have legal rights to property but will feel confident enough to claim and use those rights,” Bishwokaarma said. “I think education, legal awareness and economic opportunities are important in helping bridge the gap in land ownership.”

While Nepal’s laws have improved, Bishwokaarma said social attitudes and family practices must also change if women are to fully benefit from them. In her view, land ownership can provide security, promote independence and give women a stronger voice in family and community decisions.

“When a woman owns land or property, she often has more control over her future and has greater economic stability,” Bishwokaarma said.

Because of that, she said Nepal’s challenge is no longer expanding legal protections, but ensuring existing laws are effectively implemented and understood by the women they are intended to serve. Looking ahead, she said future governments should focus on increasing awareness of property rights, improving access to information and creating greater economic opportunities for women.

“If those areas are improved, the ownership gap may gradually become smaller,” Bishwokaarma said. “But I think social change is often slower than political change, so it may take time to see the full impact.”

title: Local restaurants, organizations aid disaster recovery in Nepal - WJAR
description: Local restaurants, organizations aid disaster recovery in Nepal  WJAR
publisher.title: WJAR
full_article:
Thousands of people are still missing after devastating flooding in Nepal, and some local organizations are stepping up to help.

The catastrophe swept through Nepal on Aug. 26, and sent people running for their lives. It decimated several cities and left them mud-covered and flattened.

Avital Sandler Loeff, executive director of the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee Disaster Relief and International Development Unit, volunteers in Nepal and shared pictures as she stood where there was once a community.

"The area is ruined," she said. "You see a lot of people sitting on the ground. Near them, there are hundreds of pictures of people missing, and they're sitting and waiting for information to come about their beloved."

Between delivering bags of hygiene kits and potable water mid-September, she turned her attention above, and says "you hear tens of helicopters in the skies, still bringing bodies, and still bringing victims of the disaster."

A resident shows a holy book as he salvages his belongings from damaged home filled with mud and debris in Devighat, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026, following the Aug. 26 flash floods. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)

A month after the catastrophe, an estimated 6,000 people are still missing. The U.S. initially mobilized $500,000 to provide emergency assistance. Luke Ortega, a deputy spokesman with the U.S. Department of State says "that number has since climbed to more than $4 million that the United States has provided, with about $3 million of that going through the World Food Program."

Those national efforts are bolstered by boots on the ground volunteers and organizations like HAPSA Nepal, led by Brown University Professor Ramu Kharel.

"We know a lot of people who had houses there. We know one of our own fellows, our organization fellows, works at the hospital that is near where this all happened, near the border up there," he says, "and I'm sure a lot of Nepali people here in Rhode Island and in the greater kind of New England area have a lot of connections there."

Kharel and HAPSA previously assisted in Nepal after the 2015 earthquake.

"From our past experience," he says, "some of the largest number of deaths that happen after flood is among the displaced families. Diarrheal diseases and sanitation issues become number one health issues and number one killers after that. So, we decided right after this happened, we got our team together on a WhatsApp call, and decided to build sanitation kits for families that could last them for about a month." He adds, "Over 3,000 families have received these kits so far."

The 1,451 known flood casualties in Nepal, comparable to the nearly 1,400 who died in Hurricane Katrina, although in a country much less equipped to sustain the effects of repeated climate disasters.

"We're anticipating displacement for months and sometimes even years," Kharel said.

Nepal Army soldiers carry a body of a worker recovered from the site of a hydropower project in Upper Trishuli, Nepal, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Kaslai Dine)

Organizers like Kharel and Loeff, and even local business owners, like Ajay Vinoben of India Restaurant Providence, are now looking ahead to supporting long-term recovery efforts.

"Nepal being a neighbor to India, it's sort of like an obligation for us to support our neighbors," Vinoben says.

There are several ways for you to support neighbors in Nepal as well.

You can join a fundraising bike ride Friday, Sept. 25 in India Point Park, visit India restaurant and purchase a gift certificate through October, or donate to supporting organizations like the Jewish Alliance of Greater Rhode Island or HAPSA Nepal.

Transporting parts of Bailey Bridge to site

Credit Simrik Air Nepal, which experienced massive flooding and thousands of deaths following the collapse of a glacier Aug. 27, is now moving from rescue operations to future redevelopment. The final rescue team fought through every obstruction inside the Chilime tunnel—the last hope for rescuing people who were trapped—to finally reach the slush-filled cavern on Sept. 16, where five bodies were located and recovered. The retrieval signals the closing phase of a mission that has stretched the limits of technical skill, endurance and India–Nepal teamwork. Along with the Nepalese Army, rescuers from the Indian Army and the National Disaster Response Force created to handle natural and man made disasters, worked in the tunnel, a government source told ENR. By about Sept 12, they had rebuilt a 1.6-km access road—400 m of it completely washed out—that was the only way to reach the tunnel, the source said. Indian and Nepalese rescue teams had to force access by crossing the river, digging through flowing slush that repeatedly buried machinery, cutting past 3-m boulders and controlling a dangerous surge of mud-mixed water with high capacity pumps. The first 125 m of the 215 m route to the cavern proved the most punishing; with 100 m of this stretch cleared through nonstop 24-hour excavation, pumping and manual crawling in near-zero visibility.

Helicopters served as Nepal’s primary lifeline during the floods, completing 1,214 sorties to evacuate 52,311 people. Total cargo delivered by air has been around 312 metric tons by the Nepal army and private helicopters. Ground route cargo exceeds 1,900 metric tons.

“The pace of work is slow. The debris has dried and turned to hard rock," said Murlidhar Joshi, director of Simrik Air, which played a major role in the rescue with a helicopter that remains dedicated to crisis flying. Last week, it delivered solar units ordered by a monastery in the region. He told ENR that every sortie had to go through the Nepal government to ensure efficiency and integration of operations.

full_article:
The Nepali government official in charge of disaster response says authorities are planning to relocate residents living in areas hit by deadly flash floods and mudflows last month to safe sites.

Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, spoke to NHK in Nepal's capital Kathmandu on Thursday. Saturday will mark one month since the disaster in the border region between Nepal and China.

Uprety said the government plans to declare riverside and other areas struck by the disaster as "not safe for settlement." He also noted that the government is selecting safe locations for long-term settlement and working to relocate schools, hospitals and other facilities.

Uprety said the relocation will likely start in the next couple of weeks and the authorities are preparing temporary housing. He added that the government intends to seek cooperation from Japan.

Uprety also said that operations to search for those believed to remain trapped in hydropower plant tunnels might end in one to two weeks.

The flash floods and mudflows have left 1,453 people dead and more than 5,600 others unaccounted for in Nepal. China's state-run media say 43 people have died and over 510 others remain missing in the country.

title: Some Climbers Refuse to End the Season as Storm Pummels Nepal - Explorersweb »
description: Some Climbers Refuse to End the Season as Storm Pummels Nepal  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
The storm from the Bay of Bengal has reached Nepal and will continue to slam the country for the next four or five days. Still, a handful of climbers stoically wait in the Base Camps of Manaslu and Dhaulagiri for conditions to improve. Others have retreated to lower altitudes but are not yet willing to call off their expeditions.

Denis Aleksenko and Artem Tsensevitsky of Russia, along with their small Manaslu team, have no intention of leaving Base Camp at all.

“Absolutely everyone has retrieved their high-altitude camps, fearing they will be destroyed by the coming snowfall,” Aleksenko wrote today. “Base Camp has been 90% dismantled and only a few scattered tents belonging to staff and steadfast climbers remain.

“We’ve stepped back from the general panic. We’re resting in Base Camp and keeping an eye on the weather. There is a 99% chance that the commercial climbing season on Manaslu is over. But that 1% chance keeps playing on our minds.”

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Down but not out

U.S.-Australia-based Climbing the 7 Summits brought its whole team back to town, but they are not yet heading home. “Our priorities are safety and success, in that order,” they wrote in social media. “We will make any final calls on our season once we have seen what actually [happens].”

Earlier today, they told ExplorersWeb that climbers, guides, and staff all relocated to either Samagaon or Kathmandu. “From that position of safety, we remain committed to giving our climbers every opportunity to summit, should one arise,” they said.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Daily forecasts from their meteorologist will guide their decisions. “There is still time in the climbing season through October,” says co-owner Caroline Pemberton.

Pemberton quoted company founder Mike Hamill, who has spent 30 years guiding in the Himalaya. Hamill has been on more than 30 expeditions to 8,000m peaks.

“In that time, he has seen teams cancel prematurely based on assumptions, while teams that were conservative and patient but stayed the course were later rewarded with safe conditions,” Pemberton explained. “He has also seen large storms forecast that then tracked away. This one may not, given its size, but no one knows for sure what the future holds.”

Logistic challenges

Elite Exped was the only Nepal-based outfitter that considered waiting for the storm to pass before concluding their season. Yesterday, they still held out some hope and remained in Base Camp.

However, they have reconsidered and called off the expedition, according to their social media today. They cite heavy snowfall that would result in murderously hard trail breaking and other difficult conditions, plus a high risk of avalanches. They added that such conditions would make “it difficult to even consider the possibility of fixing new ropes.”

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Their conclusion emphasizes that even when the weather settles and conditions improve, the mountain would require a lot of work before a large number of guided clients could proceed to the summit. With ropes buried and higher camps dismantled, it may not be worth it from an outfitter’s point of view. However, there might still be some summit chances for smaller numbers of clients with skilled guides, as long as they climb in a lighter style.

Dhaulagiri

Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary remain at 8K Expeditions’ Base Camp with two other climbers from another outfitter. A skeleton base camp crew is also there.

“We had about 20cm [of snow overnight], and it’s still snowing,” Clarke told ExplorersWeb. “Everyone here is focused on preparing for the coming storm.”

The climbers say they will have a clearer idea of what may be possible once the weather clears and they can assess its impact on the mountain.

Dhaulagiri Base Camp today. Photo: Paul Clarke

Weather warnings

It’s already raining in Kathmandu and elsewhere in Nepal. Forecasts show brief, high-intensity late-monsoon downpours, according to Nepalnews . The whole country is on alert, especially after the recent catastrophic floods that killed 1,452, according to yesterday’s ever-changing official tally. The main fears are floods and landslides. However, the media has stopped referring to the storm as a cyclone and calls it “heavy rainfall” instead.

All the mountain areas in the country are under red alert.

Weather alert chart issued by Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology today.

“The Expedition Operators’ Association Nepal (EOAN) has issued an urgent notice regarding the current and forecast weather conditions across Nepal’s mountain regions,” Nga Tenjin Sherpa of Summit Force wrote. “Forecasts indicate the possibility of heavy rainfall in lower regions, [and] snowfall and strong winds in the Himalayan areas. Expedition operators, climbers, guides, and mountain workers are requested to take necessary precautions .” Climbers on Manaslu head down to Camp 1. Photo: Summit Force Warning for both trekkers and climbers

Last year, Cyclone Montha caused havoc, but not for the 8,000m expeditions. Instead, the storm caught trekkers in the higher areas and climbers on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks. Nine people died in avalanches during that blizzard.

This time, the warnings address trekkers, travelers, and climbers. Roads and trails may be cut, and avalanches could reach the lower areas, affecting mountain trails. There could even be flash floods and landslides. Some popular trekking areas have even banned visitors:

Closure announcement for the Annapurna region.

Roland Hunter, a UK trekking outfitter with The Mountain Company, checked in with ExplorersWeb right after arriving in an already rainy Kathmandu. “Forecasts show heavier rain starting tonight until later tomorrow,” he said. “There is better dissemination of extreme weather warnings with this cyclone compared to previous years.”

Hunter said that this year, they pushed back the start dates for their camping treks to the second week of October, based on the recent pattern of cyclones or heavy monsoon rains in late September or early October.

Visitors should contact tourism offices and local operators. They can also check the weather live on webcams around Nepal, like this one at Lukla airport or this one at the Annapurna Sanctuary.

Heavy rain today at the visitors’ Annapurna Base Camp (which is lower than the actual climbers’ Base Camp). Photo: Nepal Webcam Live

Helicopters possibly grounded

Finally, the Airlines Operators Association of Nepal has told helicopter companies to keep aircraft ready for rescue work during the next five days, according to Nepal360Business . Yet, the bad weather will likely ground helicopters, eliminating the possibility of emergency evacuations.

description: Ahead of Nepal PM’s UN Address, Oil Change International Calls for Loss and Damage Funding  Oil Change International
publisher.title: Oil Change International
full_article:
Ahead of Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s address to the United Nations General Assembly, Laurie van der Burg, Public Finance Manager at Oil Change International, said:

“The people of Nepal just faced a deadly glacial flood caused by a fossil fueled climate crisis they did not create. Wealthy, high-emitting countries must urgently fill the Loss and Damage Fund, provide grant-based climate finance at the scale needed, and end the fossil fuel expansion driving this destruction. As Oil CEOs rake in record-breaking profits on the back of oil wars, governments must end fossil fuel subsidies and instead make polluters pay for their climate wreckage. On the road to COP31, governments must deliver the funding Nepal and other climate-vulnerable countries are owed so communities can recover, rebuild, transition, and prepare for the impacts ahead.”

Note to the editor:

Yesterday, Nepali diaspora members and frontline communities brought their demand for climate reparations to the UN’s doorstep.
